section.title: Austin McDonald: Behavioral Interviews, Downleveling, and How Hiring Committees Decide
section.deck: Austin McDonald, a former Meta hiring committee member, explains how leveling and hiring decisions are made and why scope-focused behavioral stories decide outcomes for senior engineers.

blocks.text: Austin McDonald, introduced by the host as a former Meta hiring committee member who led mobile hiring across the company, argues that for senior engineers the behavioral interview, and even the first recruiter conversation, is where level is decided. A candidate who wants to avoid being downleveled should know the company's rubric, choose the highest-scope stories that still fit the question, show technical, organizational and business depth, and treat every contact (recruiter, hiring manager, closing questions) as evaluative. The second half moves to interviewer dynamics, story structure, and Austin's own reflections on regret, scope and fear. Everything about Meta's process is Austin's account of their own time there and may differ at other companies or today.
blocks.heading: Senior hiring turns on scope shown in behavioral stories (Austin McDonald's view)

blocks.question: What actually happens in a hiring committee, and who touches a candidate between first contact and the final decision?
answer: Austin says that when a senior packet reached the committee, the first thing Austin read was the behavioral interview. Austin wanted to see the scope the engineer had operated at, their level of influence, insight and communication, and the size of the organization they had worked in. Committees are made up of engineers and influential engineering managers, recruited by a chair such as Austin, and work with recruiting on two decisions: hire or not, and level. Austin describes a company-wide committee that mostly does a gut check against a cross-company bar, and says that at Meta a final committee of engineering directors makes the hiring and leveling call.

The path starts with a sourcer, an entry-level recruiting job whose task is to find candidates or process referrals. The sourcer looks at the job description, years of experience and past companies. The phone screen that follows is often a coding interview, and sometimes a multiple-choice technical quiz used as a pre-filter. A clearly strong phone screen goes straight to on-site scheduling. A borderline one comes to the hiring committee for the first time, which decides whether to add a follow-up, move the person on, or pass for now.

The committee is also consulted for specialized candidates, for example a low-level C++ mobile engineer who needs a fitting system design interview, and for the choice between senior and staff. That choice changes the loop. At Meta, Austin says, staff candidates get two system design interviews, so no one could be hired at staff without them, and principal and distinguished loops add further behavioral interviews. After the on-site, the committee decides hire, level and follow-ups. Behavioral interviews generate most follow-ups, because Austin considers them among the hardest to give and to read. Committee members sometimes go with the recruiter to the directors to argue for taking a chance on someone whose packet is weak in one area but strong in a trait the company needs.

followups.question: How is a candidate's starting level first decided?
answer: Austin says the early call rests on years of experience and previous title: a staff engineer at Google will likely be brought in as staff at Meta. Many companies, Meta included, do not publish levels, so a LinkedIn profile rarely shows level, which is why years of experience carry so much weight.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: What happens to a high-titled candidate from outside big tech?
answer: Austin says sourcers and recruiters know that titles inflate in parts of the industry. A manager of 50 or 75 people at a business-oriented company might be downleveled to a team of eight or ten engineers at Meta, and individual contributors are treated the same way. Calling oneself a principal engineer on LinkedIn does not draw principal-level outreach, because different companies attach different expectations to the same level. Austin adds that a consistent industry-wide scale would be nice, but it does not exist.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: Could someone get through by inflating a title on a resume?
answer: The host posed this as a hypothetical about an unethical candidate. Austin says the first phone screen at staff and above is also a scope check: some coding, some system design, and a walk through a large shipped project. Lying convincingly is hard, because interviewers sense whether the story is true and follow-up questions expose gaps. Austin says coaching clients who recite AI-generated stories start giving vague, inconsistent answers once asked about the technology.

Austin concedes that anyone can be fooled by a good enough liar, but the on-site interviewers for staff and principal candidates are very senior and highly calibrated, so a liar would have to lie repeatedly and convincingly. Austin jokes that someone able to do that might be good enough for the job, and says that in a career of hiring thousands of people, Austin has not heard of a hire later found to have invented their background.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: The host said engineers often assume the behavioral round can be improvised. What should a candidate do to be placed at staff?
answer: Austin says the most important task, in any behavioral story and in the first chat with a recruiter, is to establish scope: what size of business problem was solved with technology, how much ambiguity was handled, and what kind of organization the candidate operated in. The recruiter call is effectively a behavioral interview, so the opening “tell me about yourself” should be the greatest hits of the resume, with metrics, and with depth and complexity.

Austin contrasts “I improved performance in the Facebook app” with an account of organizing about 100 engineers across a twelve-month performance project that hit hard technical problems, needed several staff engineers, and ended in three core principles. A candidate should convey technical depth, organizational depth and business impact, because every interviewer in the loop is listening for the same things. Crisp practice on that opening is the first place to land in the right leveling bucket.

Responding to the host's point that staff promotions also require cross-organization work, Austin agrees and says preparing for behavioral interviews makes someone a better engineer. Most of Austin's coaching clients undersell rather than exaggerate. They need to show how hard the problem was and what impact it had on the team, code quality and the organization over time. Telling the whole story takes preparation, but it is the same skill used in weekly one-on-ones and executive updates.

followups.question: Is the first recruiter call already an evaluation?
answer: The host noted that recruiters pitch the first call as a casual chat. Austin answers “always be closing”: the call is evaluative, though softer, since the recruiter wants to find a candidate who gets through. Recruiters at big companies are paid by the hires they deliver. They advocate for candidates but are not friends, and compensation is a topic to handle carefully.
Austin advises against showing up unprepared or disconnected. If not ready, reschedule and spend time preparing what to say, since that is the best route to a higher-level offer.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: Does the final chat with the hiring manager also carry signal?
answer: Austin says yes. The pressure is lower, and at companies such as Meta or Google a team-matching phase brings conversations with several managers. These chats are more social than interviews, where a long self-introduction cuts into the interviewer's time for collecting signal. The manager is asking whether they like the candidate, whether they will fit the team, and whether the candidate can solve problems like the manager's own.
So Austin recommends asking the recruiter and sourcer in advance what the manager values and what the team is working on, then telling stories that show the candidate can solve those problems.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: What is the most common mistake candidates make in compensation conversations with recruiters?
answer: Austin says they are not a negotiation expert and recommends getting advice from people who are. Their own view is that early anchoring is dangerous: when asked early about compensation expectations, a candidate should be careful, because whatever is said anchors the rest of the conversation.

Austin tells candidates to learn the local laws and says that in California and New York recruiters are required to share salary and total-comp bands, which a candidate can use to see where they sit (this legal claim is Austin's and was not checked). Austin thinks the biggest mistake is not having multiple offers. Without them, a candidate negotiates from weakness, so Austin urges candidates to time offers to land at about the same moment, even though that is more stressful and more work.
blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: If a candidate who wants only staff roles sees they are being funneled into the wrong loop, can that be corrected mid-process?
answer: Austin says that depends on the company and process, but it is a good conversation to have with the recruiter. Companies uplevel candidates as well as downlevel them, and recruiters will usually try to keep someone in the process. Austin suggests pushing to complete as much of the evaluation as possible for the desired level up front, so that follow-up interviews and late changes are not needed. If a team offers only a lower level, it depends on the job and total compensation, but Austin would aim to excel and then ask for consideration at the higher level.

Austin names two methods. The first is to anchor every conversation at the higher level, starting with “tell me about yourself” and then in the behavioral and system design interviews, so that interviewers see large-scope projects and impact and reset what they expect from the rest of the interview. The second is story choice. Behind every behavioral question is a question the interviewer actually cares about: is the candidate operating at the expected level? Interviewers forget the details quickly.

Austin says their book gives four considerations for choosing a story, and scope comes first. The candidate's job is to leave having told the most important stories of their career, and since the interviewer drives, to steer the conversation toward the signal that best represents them.
blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: What do senior, staff and principal scope look like, and how should a candidate express them?
answer: Austin first says to research the specific company's level expectations, then offers a simple rubric for big-tech-style companies, shown in the table below. Levels are really about how much ambiguity a person can handle. Austin notes that the ambiguity facing an intern differs from the ambiguity facing a chief executive, and says that difference is what separates both levels and pay.

Staff versus senior comes down to breadth of impact: a whole team or several teams rather than a small project. Stories involve working across a large organization. For that reason Austin thinks startup engineers struggle to reach staff unless they were founders, because a few engineers and one stakeholder limit how much organizational leadership they can show.

Austin adds two more things to quantify or mention. For technical complexity, a candidate should give a sense of the time involved, the risk, how many people were consulted, and how hard it would have been to back out of a decision. For leadership, which engineers often forget because they love to talk about technology, a candidate should describe influence, getting concessions from other teams, aligning roadmaps, and mentoring people to make the team and organization better. Austin recommends reflecting on one's own career to identify what differentiates it, and talking about those things.

followups.question: How should a specialist who solves problems no one else can describe their scope?
answer: The host asked about people who push the industry forward on their own. Austin says to start with business impact, which technology-focused engineers find hard. There was a reason the technology was needed and a context around it, and Austin encourages people to ask what Steve Jobs would say about the advance and why the project was critical to the company.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: Is it too much to say that a team of staff engineers failed before the candidate succeeded?
answer: The host said that framing works when a manager says it in a promotion committee, but that a candidate saying it about themselves may sound like too much. Austin disagrees outright. In Austin's view behavioral interviewers are pattern matchers, and having solved problems others could not is one of the patterns for a higher level.

Austin finds it fine to say a candidate was the third owner of a project and where earlier owners failed, as long as the point is not to boast but to show insight into why those efforts failed, whether a product-market fit that did not work or a technical approach that did not work. Austin sees that judgment and reflection as a mark of seniority, and says many candidates simply tell a problem-solved story with no lesson, which Austin treats as a sign of someone below the level.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: Is it unfair that candidates who sell themselves well do better?
answer: The host noted that commenters complain about people who manage optics, and that promotion content draws the same objection. Austin replies that this is how people work, in careers and in personal relationships alike: saying “can't you feel that I love you” does not work, and behaviors must be shown and communicated.

Austin calls self-advocacy an unpleasant but worthwhile tax on progress that candidates can skip only by giving up staff-level promotion or hiring. Austin tells people that a principal engineering job is about a million dollars a year in compensation, so they should be fully ready for the process.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.title: Austin McDonald's rubric of scope by level
rows: Takes a task from the manager or ticket system, completes it, and comes back for the next.
A feature (many tasks, a couple of weeks)
Delivers a feature end to end.
Leads and delegates, often through mid-level or junior engineers, with communication and organization.
A goal such as an engagement or revenue goal
Coordinates several projects, working across teams and a large organization, with influence and mentoring.
Responsibility spans many goals, projects, features and tasks; Austin says names for these levels vary.
Responsibility for an entire business containing many organizations.

blocks.question: Who actually makes the hiring decision?
answer: Austin lists the decision points. The sourcer, who decides from a LinkedIn profile whether to contact someone, is distinct from the recruiter, who takes over after the phone screen, runs the negotiation, organizes the loop and advocates before the committee. The phone screener is another decision point, whether a sourcer's multiple-choice question or an engineer's coding screen.

The hiring committee then decides, usually by consensus and sometimes by vote, whether to hire at a level, add a follow-up, or drop the candidate. Two or three engineering directors above the committee make the final call, again mostly by consensus and sometimes by vote.
blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: Did Austin ever see bias in a hiring committee, such as nepotism, and how much do referrals matter?
answer: Austin has never seen overt nepotism or bribery, but has seen referrals play a huge role, especially when the referrer is senior or shows up in the committee room to advocate. The referrer's seniority matters: a VP or director risks personal reputation, while a note that someone knew a candidate at school carries little weight. Content matters as well. A referral saying the person worked directly with the candidate and listing specific strengths helps much more, so Austin tells candidates to write the referral for the referrer.

Austin says referrals matter most for candidates on the bubble. Austin's own phone screens went poorly, and Austin believes a follow-up interview was granted because a former schoolmate who had worked with them directly had referred them.

followups.question: Could a very strong referral rescue a lukewarm interview performance?
answer: The host described a candidate with a lukewarm result and the strongest possible VP referral. Austin says referrals help on the bubble, usually by winning a follow-up, and Austin has never seen a general consensus not to hire overturned for an engineer. It may happen more in leadership hiring, which Austin calls a different matter. At senior manager and director level, Austin thinks who you know sometimes matters more than raw performance, because the number of decision makers shrinks and they are easier to influence.
Austin adds that a good hiring process is not like that: it identifies what makes people successful and evaluates for it without bias.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: How well does interview performance predict performance on the job?
answer: Austin says the committee did not track how many interviews someone passed. It looked at the interviewer's stated confidence in a hire-and-level decision, and that confidence correlated with later performance. Austin reads this as evidence that calibrated interviewers who have run hundreds of interviews sense what good looks like even when it is hard to define, and that a rubric reduces bias without removing the gut feel.

Austin also notes that some candidates excel in interviews and then do poorly, and others look rocky and then do well. Interviewing is a skill separate from the job, and Austin says candidates need to spend time getting good at it.
blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: What does the behavioral rubric look like, and how should a candidate use it?
answer: Austin says it varies by company. Well-run large companies often employ industrial-psychology PhDs, called selection scientists, who study what makes engineers successful and codify it into signal areas. At Meta, according to Austin, there are five: driving results, embracing ambiguity, resolving conflicts, growing continuously and communicating effectively. These are not Meta's company values. Candidates should ask the recruiter for the rubric in advance or search for it.

Austin groups the typical five to eight items into eight broader signal areas, described in their book, and tells candidates to categorize their stories by those areas. Inside the interview the core loop is decode, select, deliver: work out why the question is being asked and which area it probes, select a story that supplies that signal, and tell it engagingly. At smaller companies a formal rubric may not exist. There Austin suggests relying on company values and asking recruiters or team members what makes engineers successful and what the hiring process looks for.

followups.question: How can one story serve different questions, and what does the interviewer need from the candidate?
answer: The host says that as an interviewer of hundreds of candidates, including engineering managers, the host often asked a targeted question and watched candidates talk past it into a rehearsed spiel, leaving a blank in the rubric. The host sees the interview as a mutual exercise in filling out that rubric.

Austin agrees and offers a movie-trailer image, credited to PM behavioral coach Robert Hamilton. One story may contain action, romance, ambiguity, communication and conflict, and the candidate can re-cut it into a trailer that fits the question. That has to happen early, in the opening context. Austin says candidates should treat themselves as partners helping the interviewer reach the signal sought.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.title: Austin McDonald's decode, select, deliver loop

steps.title: Decode
steps.text: Listen for why the question is being asked and which signal area, or company value, the interviewer is probing.

steps.title: Select
steps.text: Choose, from stories already sorted by signal area, the one that gives that signal at the highest scope that fits.

steps.title: Deliver
steps.text: Tell it as a short arc, putting the part that answers the question near the start so the interviewer gets the signal early.

blocks.caption: Editorial summary of the loop Austin describes while discussing the behavioral rubric; the step wording is condensed from Austin's account.

blocks.question: How should candidates tailor behavioral stories for OpenAI and Anthropic?
answer: Austin starts by mapping stories onto the eight general signal areas, because most company values reduce to them, and then adds whatever the company's own values contribute. For OpenAI, Austin reads “act with humility” as growth: taking feedback and improving yourself and those around you. “Feel the AGI” is outside the eight areas. Austin reads it as being optimistic about what AI could do for the world.

For Anthropic, the caption renders a value as “hold light and shade”, which Austin takes to mean understanding both the positive and negative implications of AI. A story about using AI at Anthropic should mention the potential harms the candidate thought about and how they assessed and mitigated them. Without that, Austin says, the interviewers will not feel comfortable hiring. At OpenAI a candidate who is not AI-forward or excited about new domains for AI will interest them less. These are Austin's readings of the values, not official definitions.
blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: What are the most common behavioral interview mistakes for senior engineers?
answer: Austin lists several. First, the wrong stories, meaning stories that do not match the target scope. Second, too much context: senior people are good communicators and tend to talk, but only the context needed to understand the behaviors is useful. If about thirty seconds pass without an action in the story, Austin suggests the candidate is giving too much backstory or technical detail. Work stories are not exciting, Austin admits, so the action must keep moving.

Third, inviting uncharitable readings. Interviewers hiring a senior leader are risk-averse, so a candidate should think defensively. Saying the codebase had heavy technical debt may sound like a good story, but a senior engineer in the room invites the question of how it got that way. Austin recommends adding the judgment behind the situation, for example that the team was a startup that had to close its next funding round and so accepted the debt, then chose to prioritize paying it down.

Fourth, too little on non-technical work: mentoring, organizing, delegating, influencing the roadmap, resolving conflicts, working across teams and managing up. Fifth, long, multi-year stories need an organized shape. Austin suggests opening with a short table of contents (the business context, then perhaps five parts such as proposing the idea, aligning stakeholders, solving hard problems and a long rollout), so the candidate can return to the key parts after interruptions.

followups.question: How should a candidate choose which story to tell?
answer: Austin gives four criteria in order. Scope comes first, which Austin says surprises people who assume relevance is first: how can a big-scope story fit the question? Relevance is second, since a story about an unambiguous project cannot answer a question on ambiguity. Recency is third: stories from the last two to three years are fine, beyond three or four years needs a strong reason, and the limit stretches with seniority, so a principal with a 30-year career may use a ten-year-old story. Uniqueness is fourth: across several behavioral rounds a candidate should avoid repeating the same story, for example keeping the project deep dive separate from the general ambiguity answer.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: Is it acceptable to answer like a politician and steer toward a stronger story?
answer: The host compared this to a politician delivering a rehearsed answer that fills in the rubric rather than the question asked. Austin says, unfortunately, yes. The aim is to leave having shown the most business value and problem solving, and strictly answering the narrow question can leave a bigger story untold.

Austin's example is a question about a conflict with a product manager. A candidate can say they had one and outline it, then offer that a longer conflict with a director of engineering, involving data collection and many meetings, might be more interesting, and ask whether to tell that instead. The interviewer may constrain the candidate back to the smaller story, but the interviewer may also only be gathering conflict-resolution signal.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: How can a candidate tell whether they are talking too long?
answer: Austin says interviewers differ. Some, like Austin, listen and take in what the candidate finds interesting. Others interrupt, turn a detail over, ask many follow-ups or move quickly between questions. Candidates should be emotionally prepared for the second type, who can make a candidate feel they are failing when the interviewer is just bouncing around.

Austin advises reading cues such as eye contact and note-taking, and if engagement drops, pausing to ask whether this is what the interviewer wants. A calibrated interviewer will interrupt even if rude in order to collect signal, but weaker ones need the candidate to make stopping easy. Austin recommends talking for no more than two to four minutes at a time, since a monologue longer than four or five minutes has to be very good.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: How should a candidate split preparation time across coding, system design and behavioral rounds?
answer: Austin says most people spend too much time on coding and too little on system design and behavioral, which are murkier to prepare for. For juniors, the technical signal matters most, and the behavioral focus should be on thinking, motivations and ideas tried, as signals of future impact, since juniors have fewer accomplishments.

For mid-level engineers, Austin says the old approach of focusing only on technical work and not flubbing the behavioral no longer works. Austin gives two reasons: layoffs have produced many candidates, so one must shine across all interview types, and more technical work is being done with agentic coding, so employers want mid-level engineers who own problems end to end and keep learning as engineering changes quickly. Austin says that ownership and growth show up in the behavioral interview. Coding practice should come early because coding assessments come first, but some weeks before the on-site a candidate should choose core stories, study values and the rubric, and make sure each key area has a story.

From senior up, Austin says it mostly comes down to behavioral. For a staff packet Austin went straight to the behavioral interview, since there are only so many ways to design a web crawler or solve two-sum, and the behavioral shows organizational impact, influence, conflict handling, scope and business impact. At staff-plus levels, extra rounds may include a cross-functional partner such as a PM or a project deep dive. Austin sees the technical rounds there as checkmarks to pass and the behavioral ones as what gets someone hired.

Austin thinks most people underinvest in behavioral preparation, which takes at least a few weeks. Staff candidates and above should start when they start LeetCode, work on positioning stories, get feedback, and do mocks with a friend or professional. For in-demand companies such as Meta, OpenAI or Anthropic, Austin recommends a mock interviewer calibrated to that company who can give a feel for its culture.

followups.question: Can a packet with a modest technical result and a strong behavioral result still go through?
answer: Austin says yes at the highest levels. At staff, principal and manager levels, where less day-to-day coding is expected, the committee would discount a weak coding performance. That is much harder for junior candidates.

Austin tells of a candidate whose accomplishments were limited and technical performance only okay. Austin kept seeing ideas the candidate had tried to push even though a manager disagreed or the organization blocked them. Austin pushed for the hire and says the person later became a staff engineer. Austin's reading is that the behavioral interview assesses a slope of growth, even for juniors.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: How much does subjective likeability matter, and how does presence affect the outcome?
answer: Austin says it scales with level. At big companies, behavioral interviews for juniors are structured, with forms, to reduce the “beer test” effect. For seniors the interviewer expects the person to influence others on the job, so how they come across counts. Austin describes a Silicon Valley quality of “casual excellence”: looking calm yet sharply competent. A disheveled or nervous candidate who cannot be present is giving signal about how they will show up in meetings and before a CEO.

Austin adds that cultural norms differ by country and company. The conversation here is about a Silicon Valley or Seattle style that opens with playful banter and then turns to hard-hitting questions, and candidates should learn the expectations of the place they are applying to.

followups.question: How can a staff engineer who is not a people person come across strongly?
answer: Austin starts from the idea that the inside shows on the outside, so the work begins with belief rather than a mask. Austin cites a recent podcast by the author of a book on Silicon Valley etiquette, named in the captions as Sam Lesson (spelling unverified), who stressed lowering heart rate before the conversation. Austin points out that a company that will be around has other chances, so a candidate can give themselves permission to make mistakes and appear calmer.

The second belief is empathy: the interviewer wants to find a great engineer, is not an enemy, and is a human who would be glad to work with the candidate. On the outside, Austin suggests dressing one notch up, checking the video background, and showing care in the first minutes rather than waiting passively. A candidate who is not extroverted can still let their regard for people show through a warm greeting and stated enthusiasm. Austin recommends practicing that opening in mock interviews, noting that the interviewer may be nervous too and that a hiring manager or leader shapes the candidate's view of the team.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: Does a curt, concise candidate or a warm, bubbly one score better?
answer: The host posed this contrast. Austin says it depends on who conducts the interview, and that Austin would favor the warmer person because Austin likes to engage. But rapport does not mean bubbliness, it means connecting with the other person. A candidate should start positive and energetic, then read the interviewer. Someone who skips the introduction and goes straight to “tell me about a time” wants efficiency, so the candidate should be efficient. Someone who opens with several minutes of weather and sports is a different type, and the candidate should match that energy.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: Which counts more, the first impression or the last impression?
answer: Austin says that if forced to choose, the beginning. Austin often decides within the first ten or fifteen minutes whether to hire, since Austin opens with the biggest-scope questions (favorite project, most ambiguous project, something proud of). If Austin would like to see that performance replicated in the organization, the rest of the interview is a check on other areas such as conflict resolution and growth.

The ending still matters, mainly through the candidate's questions. Austin says candidates often prepare stories but then ask something generic like a day in the life of an engineer, which is similar everywhere. Questions drawn from real thought about the team, organization, product and company, and that help the candidate decide whether to join, leave the impression of an engaged candidate.

followups.question: What share of the outcome is already set early in the interview?
answer: Austin says no social science has been applied directly to tech interviews, and one cannot simply transfer research from a fast-food company. Austin recalls research saying roughly 40 percent of decisions are made in the first 15 percent, about the first ten minutes (Austin's recollection, not verified). In Austin's own experience it is rare to decide against someone early and then be won back at minute 38. More common is feeling unsure, then writing notes against the rubric, which is meant to move the decision from a gut reaction to something more deliberate.

If Austin decided early, it was hard for the candidate to overcome, usually because of poor story choice, work below the expected level, or weak storytelling. The host adds from experience that interviewers seem to zone out halfway once they have already decided, which makes the first half important, and that the closing questions are also evaluative.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: What makes a good question to ask at the end?
answer: Austin says everything is evaluative, from the recruiter call to the closing questions. A candidate should start from what matters to them: worry about the company's long-term product prospects, or, for career growth and a supportive manager, a request such as asking the manager to describe helping someone grow from one level to the next. Technology-stack questions seem more junior to Austin, though in an AI context a question about model construction or evaluation could be strong. One of Austin's favorites is what makes someone in this role successful, which signals interest in succeeding.

Austin would not try to impress with a deep question, but would let a genuine concern read as depth. Questions about the conversation for the role, or about free food, may matter to the candidate but do not belong with a behavioral interviewer.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: What are the best ways to tell a behavioral story with the least effort?
answer: Austin says a story needs an arc, with a beginning, middle and end, and must deliver the signal area the interviewer is after: past behavior that can be repeated in the new organization. STAR (situation, task, action, result) is the best-known shortcut. Austin does not love it but says that anyone with prepared STAR stories the night before should use them, since they give an arc, context for the actions, and results.

Austin prefers CALR: context, actions, results, learnings. The difference between situation and task is not useful in a long project, which has many tasks, so context followed by actions is simpler. For senior engineers STAR leaves no room for reflection, judgment or learning, and Austin looks for whether the candidate can see what made them successful or not and apply it forward.

followups.question: How should a candidate adapt the length of an answer to the question?
answer: Austin says senior candidates manage time. A “trunk” question such as a project that was really ambiguous invites a longer story. A “branch” question, such as whom the candidate spoke to for a piece of information, seeks a communication signal and deserves something shorter than a full STAR or CALR story. A “leaf” question, such as which framework was used, only needs the answer before moving on. Austin says detecting how long the interviewer wants to listen is both a mark of seniority and a way to manage the interview.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: What matters more, what the candidate says or how they say it?
answer: Austin says mostly what, because engineering interviews are structured and engineers value substance. A candidate who sounds confident and positive but shows no structured approach to ambiguity or conflict will not win support. Form follows function.

Austin adds that delivery matters more at senior levels, because senior people must tell engaging status stories, for example when a VP asks how a project is going. Details belong only when they serve a purpose, such as technical depth or, in a cross-team story, how another tech lead's hostile look showed the candidate pushing through resistance. Most candidates, Austin thinks, need more work on basic story structure and on naming the repeatable actions they took.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: The host asked Austin to explain, in terms of scope, why Austin was promoted to M2 at Meta.
answer: Austin says getting to M2 meant solving hard problems in recruiting, with the most important being diversity. Austin left a team building products for teenagers, which Austin calls a hard time for Facebook, to lead teams in the internal recruiting products organization that supports candidates, recruiters and sourcers. What drew Austin was a team working to hire more diverse engineers, and Austin was motivated by opening technology, which Austin calls the largest wealth opportunity, to more people.

Austin says a product team cannot decide school curricula or all hiring decisions, but could move the needle by improving interview preparation, and credits that with helping diversity hiring at Meta. Austin also supported other teams in building high-quality candidate data in Facebook's applicant tracking system. The host heard multiple teams, an ambiguous problem and strong self-motivation. Austin agrees and adds company-wide impact from leading the iOS and Android recruiting pipelines, which scaled Austin beyond the teams directly managed. These are Austin's own account of their record.
blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: Looking back on big tech, does Austin regret anything?
answer: Austin does not regret leaving and says they enjoyed working with wonderful people. The regret is the anxiety brought into teams and into their own life. Austin points out that no one at the end of life wishes they had gotten a few more percent of an engagement number, and says people value relationships and connection.

Austin says they made conscious choices to favor life experience over career but were not always honest with themselves about the trade-offs in pay, progression and status. Since leaving big tech to support a spouse's business, income has dropped. Before leaving, Austin decided to accept lower cash flow in exchange for more time with their kids and more community volunteering, and has returned to that choice when money was tight. Austin wishes to have made that kind of values-driven decision earlier.

followups.question: What did being dishonest with oneself look like?
answer: Austin describes frustration and at times bitterness when others were promoted or got jobs. Austin says the honest answer was that those people moved teams faster and worked harder, while Austin prioritized family and community. Austin does not think people can have everything: some may be able to be a level-seven IC and leave at 5:00, depending on talent and skills built, but for most people accomplishing something extraordinary takes extraordinary steps.
Austin says that deciding what mattered, including what their children would remember about them in ten or fifteen years, was clarifying.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

followups.question: Did that clarity remove the feelings of envy?
answer: Austin says the feelings return on a semi-regular basis, especially in Silicon Valley where people stack wealth quickly. Each time Austin asks whether that is what they want. Being aligned with one's own values, with a mission statement or vision for life, is what Austin finds satisfying.
followups.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: What is the best career advice Austin ever received?
answer: Austin says it was the importance of creating scope. Many people wait for someone to give them the opportunity, but a manager once told Austin that to get an M2 role, Austin had to create an M2-scope team and solve problems of that size. Advancing does not mean doing the same thing better. It means doing something different, which is creating more scope and room for the organization to succeed.

Austin adds a test: what is the VP saying about your project, and if the VP is not telling peers or their manager, is it the right work? Candidates already work backwards from the signal area they want to show in an interview and from the packet they want in a promotion. Austin suggests working backwards in the same way from what leadership should say about the accomplishment, then finding a way to achieve it. The host adds that promotions built on self-created scope are the most satisfying because they need no one's permission.
blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald

blocks.question: What advice would Austin give a younger self just after college?
answer: Austin says imposter syndrome held them back. After completing a computer science PhD, Austin spent summers doing university research while peers took industry internships at places like Google or Facebook, because Austin did not want to go through interviews and risk rejection. Austin loves their career and would not change much, but says that fear slowed their understanding of how big organizations and large codebases work, coming from academia.
Austin's summary advice is simple: do not give in to fear.
blocks.speaker: Austin McDonald
